reader: AI reader 32 (targeted check at the stated place)

sources_read.parrott_2013: PDF, in-press proof pp. 1-19 (text extraction plus rendered p. 5 for paragraph structure); proof line numbers used as printed in the margins.
sources_read.parrott_2011: PDF pp. 1365-1368 (the letter ends on p. 1367; the Fisk et al. letter beginning on p. 1368 was read only to separate it).
sources_read.lyvers_2011: Publisher full text (HTML), https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1360-0443.2010.03344.x, read in this reader's own browser tab (tab-7): all four paragraphs, declaration of interests and the 18 references.
sources_read.cowan_2012: PMC full text PMC3280662, read in the same tab: all five paragraphs, author information, article notes, acknowledgments, competing interests and references.
sources_read.mithoefer_2003: PDF pp. 1503-1505, letter and reply on pp. 1504-1505; p. 1504 rendered to count the reply's paragraphs.
sources_read.barnett_2021: PDF, online-first version, article pp. 1-7; p. 5 rendered to count the Discussion's paragraphs; Tables 1-2 checked.
sources_read.cross_checks: Halpern et al. (2011) PMC3053129 (Tables 1-4 and Discussion) and McCann et al. (1994) PDF pp. 132-133 (Table 4) were opened to check statements made about them.

results.note: Proof lines 355-379 (2nd paragraph of §3.2, which begins at line 347 on p. 5 and ends on p. 6): Laws and Kokkalis (2007), 26 studies with calculable effect sizes, d -0.63 short-term, -0.87 long-term, -1.00 verbal, -0.27 visual; Rogers et al. (2009), review of over one hundred neurocognitive studies, deficits against both non-using and polydrug-using controls with strength varying by task; Nulsen et al. (2010), worse performance in all memory domains. All four d values, the study count and the role (supports) match.

§3.5, 3rd paragraph, proof lines 587-605 on p. 7: seven variables meta-analysed, six memory measures (RAVLT immediate and delayed word recall, RBMT immediate and delayed prose recall, digit span forwards and backwards) lower against both control types, IQ the seventh and not lower than polydrug controls, and the review's own sentence that the deficits were generally strongest against non-using controls. Matches.

p. 1365, 2nd paragraph (left column continuing into the right): marked variation across studies; pooled digit span P=0.017 against polydrug controls; verbal immediate recall composite over 27 published studies P<0.001; six of seven meta-analysed variables lower, NART IQ the exception. Every number and the role (qualifies) match.

§3.4, 1st paragraph (which runs from proof line 462), Murphy et al. (2009) summarized at lines 476-493 on p. 6: 33 studies, performance normal in most, executive-shifting and most inhibition tasks unaffected, deficits mainly in updating verbal information and in visuospatial tasks needing processing beyond storage and retrieval. Matches word for word in substance.

§3.5, 5th paragraph, proof lines 634-654 on p. 8: simple skills generally unimpaired, deficits not universally apparent, digit span and the verbal immediate-recall composite a mixture of significant and non-significant individual studies with significant pooled estimates, variation attributed to lifetime dosage, sample size, participant selection and control of error variance. Matches.

p. 1366, 5th running-text paragraph: the five tests and p values as printed in the letter (spatial span forwards P<0.04, digit-symbol P<0.02, vocabulary P<0.01, digits backwards P<0.05, non-dominant-hand pegboard P<0.02); the rejection of the authors' chance reading; and the remark that trail-making B and California verbal learning did not differ. Matches.

p. 1366, 6th and 7th paragraphs: subgroups at fewer than 50 and 50+ lifetime occasions, 'did not generally differ' with the moderate subgroup sometimes more impaired, 6 of the 22 in the heavier subgroup at 150+ occasions, subgroup lifetime rates not presented; pegboard unimpaired with the dominant hand, P=0.02 for the whole group and P=0.003 for the heavier subgroup, judged probably chance by the study's authors. Matches.

Publisher HTML, 1st paragraph: 15 tests 'reported previously by others to differentiate ecstasy users from controls'; only the Revised Strategy Applications Test a clear indication of poorer performance, in heavy but not moderate use; selection for low exposure to other illicit drugs and alcohol; controls from the same rave subculture; adjustment for demographic and other factors including ADHD. Matches.

Publisher HTML, 2nd paragraph: low serotonergic functioning linked to impulsivity, impulsivity to low prefrontal activation, reward sensitivity, signs of frontal dysfunction and heavier substance use; a prospective study in which a test score in people who had not used ecstasy predicted later use. Small point: the commentary's own words are 'higher impulsivity on a neuropsychological test'; 'decision-making' comes from the title of its reference 12 (Schilt et al., 2009). The extracted text is accurate but names the measure from the reference rather than the sentence.

§3.5, 4th paragraph, proof lines 606-633, running from p. 7 to p. 8: Halpern et al. (2004) light subgroup no differences and heavy subgroup lower on Wisconsin card sorting, Stroop interference and the strategy test; Yip and Lee (2005) Hong Kong sample with polydrug histories excluded; Halpern et al. (2011) few deficits overall with spatial span forwards and digit span backwards attributed to the heavier subgroup. The last attribution is wrong at source, as the anchor says: Halpern's Table 3 gives p=0.18 and 0.15 in the heavier subgroup, and Table 2 p=0.04 and 0.05 in the whole group (checked in PMC3053129).

§3.2, 4th paragraph, proof lines 401-418 on p. 6: 149 almost-naive at baseline, 23 tested after a mean of 13.5 tablets against 43 cannabis-using controls, most tasks no difference, figural visual recognition poorer (Wagner et al., 2013); 188 ecstasy-naive, 58 who used a mean of 3.2 tablets against 60 who did not, no baseline difference, poorer immediate and delayed verbal recall and verbal recognition (Schilt et al., 2007). The review's '18-36 months' is wrong: Schilt et al. (PDF p. 731) report 11.1 (SD 6.2) months in the ecstasy group and 19.1 (SD 7.5) in controls, t=6.30, p<.001. The anchor states this correctly.

§3.2, 3rd paragraph, proof lines 380-400 on p. 6: 15 people retested after a year, average lifetime use 19 to 55 occasions, decline on Rivermead paragraph recall but not on two WAIS subtests; at 2 years, 8 who stopped (19.9 to 22.9) and 7 who continued (17.4 to 9.2). The closing sentence about the absence of a retested comparison group is the editors' observation, not the review's words, and is correct: no control group is mentioned for either report.

§2.2, 5th paragraph (the paragraph begins at proof line 264 with Di Iorio et al.; the de Win sentences run at lines 276-294 on p. 5, checked on the rendered page): 188 followed, 59 using by the 17-month follow-up (mean 6.0 tablets, median 2.0) against 56, no SERT difference attributed to the very low dose, differences in cerebral blood volume, fractional anisotropy and apparent diffusion. Matches.

corrected.extracted: As summarized: 49 people with moderate ecstasy use against 50 people who did not use it; serotonin transporter binding lower in every region of the cerebral cortex (range -19% to -46%) and in the hippocampus (-21%), related to the extent of use (years, maximum dose); recent use confirmed by hair analysis, with other psychoactive drug use, sex, a gene polymorphism and chronic tolerance monitored; the review adds that studies of heavier use also found subcortical reductions (Kish et al., 2010).

results.note: Everything in the anchor is at the stated place except the last clause. The occipital lobe's mean 46% reduction and the caudorostral gradient are not in §2.2, 2nd paragraph; they appear on p. 8, §3.6 Visual information processing, 1st paragraph (proof lines 661-669), where the review quotes Kish et al. on the gradient and gives the 46% figure. Move that clause or drop it; the rest (49 vs 50, -19% to -46%, -21%, years and maximum dose, hair analysis, confounds monitored) is verbatim at p. 4, proof lines 186-210.

§2.2, 3rd paragraph, proof lines 211-238 on p. 4: Erritzoe et al. (2011) neocortex -56%, pallidostriatum -19%, amygdala -32%, correlated with lifetime MDMA exposure, no change in the hallucinogen-preferring group; Kish et al. (2000) post-mortem case, striatal serotonin -60% to -77% with normal dopamine, the person having also used cocaine and heroin. All five numbers match.

§2.2, 1st paragraph, proof lines 161-185, beginning on p. 3 and continuing on p. 4: not every study found deficits; variation attributed to lifetime dosage, duration of abstinence, radioligand, brain region, gender, polydrug use and sample size; the mid-2000s criticism of marker specificity and other methodological issues; Cowan (2007) quoted for lower SERT density as the most robust finding. Matches, role qualifies.

Same place as n=44 (p. 5, proof lines 276-294). The contradicting role is right: no SERT difference in the 59 against 56 comparison, and the quoted conclusion that the authors could not exclude that ecstasy even in low doses is neurotoxic is at proof lines 289-294.

p. 1366 right column into p. 1367, 8th paragraph: Cowan's review (the letter's reference 23) for lower SERT density as the most robust finding; 49 abstinent against 50 non-using controls, every cortical region -19% to -46%, hippocampus -21%, associated with cumulative lifetime use and maximum single-occasion use, remaining after control for confounds including other drug use, and correlated with cognitive performance. Matches.

PMC HTML, 4th paragraph: the author accepts that impulsivity may predispose to use, states that MDMA has a well-established ability to cause serotonin neurotoxicity in non-human primates and that he is aware of no evidence that humans are less vulnerable. Note for the editor: that sentence carries no citation of its own, and the paragraph does cite two human studies (Salomon et al., 2011, functional connectivity; de Win et al., 2007, impulsivity) without any numbers, so 'he gives no human measurement in support' is right as to measurements but he does point to human studies.

p. 2, Introduction, 5th paragraph (counting the paragraph that runs across the first column break as one): September 2002, Ricaurte, McCann and associates at Johns Hopkins, NIDA-funded, MDMA given to 10 non-human primates to model human use, imaging reported severe dopaminergic and less severe serotonergic neurotoxicity, two of the animals died, the dopaminergic finding novel and raising the possibility of parkinsonism. Matches, and the anchor rightly attributes the two deaths to these authors.

p. 2, Introduction, 8th paragraph: September 2003, one year after publication, Science issued a retraction in which Ricaurte and colleagues wrote that methamphetamine rather than MDMA had been used to treat all but one study animal because of a labelling error; MAPS then asked NIDA to investigate all work done since the mislabelled supply was received. Matches.

p. 3, Results, 1st paragraph: 26 of 50 (52%) covered the publication, 20 (40%) the retraction, 6 (12%) the retraction only, 14 of 26 (54%) both; circulation not associated with coverage of the publication (p=.25) or the retraction (p=.84). Every figure matches.

p. 3, Results, 2nd paragraph: 482 (SD 303; range 69-1260) against 396 (SD 193; 86-837), and 550 (SD 271) against 386 (SD 205) in the 14 newspapers covering both events. The statement that no test of these differences is reported is correct for the whole paper.

p. 3 Results, 3rd paragraph and Table 2 on p. 4: both universal components in 20 of 20; 14 (70%) controversy, 13 (65%) criticism, 11 (55%) animals died, 7 (35%) earlier serotonergic research, 7 (35%) political motives, 4 (20%) a critic's quotation; no component significant, Fisher p from 0.06 to 1.00. I recomputed eight of the Fisher tests from the table's counts (0.61, 0.35, 0.16, 0.06, 0.61, 1.00, 0.55, 0.61) and they agree with the printed values.

p. 1504: the letter (single paragraph, left column) argues from the high mortality that the regimen was not a common recreational one and questions the interspecies scaling model; the reply's 1st paragraph (middle column, continuing at the top of the right column) states that interspecies scaling was not used in these studies and that one of ten monkeys died of complications related to hyperthermia, so that conclusions about mortality are premature given the sample size. Paragraph structure checked on the rendered page.

corrected.extracted: The authors note that the retraction was issued late on a Friday afternoon, giving low-key coverage (quoting a Nature editorial), and list as limitations that archives could not be searched for all of the 50 largest US newspapers, that the AAAS press release accompanying the retraction could not be obtained, and that the placement of stories within newspapers was not analysed.

results.note: The late-Friday quotation is in the Discussion's 4th paragraph and the limitations in its 7th, both on p. 5 (paragraph breaks checked on the rendered page: the 'In this case, the initial AAAS press release...' text at the top of p. 5 is unindented and continues the 3rd paragraph from p. 4). The clause about a university announcement and a press release from the publisher's association is not at either place: the Johns Hopkins Gazette announcement and the AAAS press release are described in the Introduction, 6th paragraph (p. 2), and the AAAS release again in the Discussion, 3rd paragraph (pp. 4-5).

p. 1504, middle of the letter's single paragraph: two in vivo imaging reports of the dopamine transporter (refs 7, 8), one post-mortem examination of an individual (ref 9), and earlier studies by Ricaurte and McCann said to have found no reduced dopamine metabolites in cerebrospinal fluid (refs 10-12). Matches. The editor should keep the card's reporting issue beside it: ref 11 is McCann et al. (1994), whose Table 4 (PDF p. 133) gives CSF HVA 19.4 (SD 7.8) against 27.4 (21.3) ng/ml, group effect F(1,52)=6.9, p=.01, with the difference in women.

p. 1504, Response, 3rd paragraph (right column; the reply has five paragraphs, checked on the rendered page): groups unselected for pattern of use were likely heterogeneous so dopamine markers including the transporter would not be expected to differ, and CSF HVA is neither a sensitive nor a specific marker of dopamine neurotoxicity. Matches.

p. 5, Discussion, 6th paragraph: evidence of MDMA-induced dopaminergic toxicity in humans has not materialized since the retraction, and regulatory agencies have determined that MDMA's potential therapeutic benefits outweigh its risks in research settings, with Doblin et al. (2014) the only citation attached. The second author of this article is a co-author of that commentary, as the anchor says.
p. 2, Introduction: the novel dopaminergic finding and the possibility of parkinsonism in the 5th paragraph, the September 2003 retraction and the labelling error in the 8th. Both as stated.

p. 1, Abstract, proof lines 9-22: neurotoxicity well established in laboratory animals; lower SERT binding in abstinent people who use ecstasy; declarative memory, prospective memory and higher cognitive skills often impaired; deficits often related to lifetime dosage, slight in light use and more pronounced in heavy use; deficits across a wide range of biobehavioral functions with a serotonergic component. Matches.

p. 15, §6.2, 6th paragraph, proof lines 1522-1539: the question of endurance over time cannot be answered on current evidence, there are some indications that the problems endure (Morgan et al., 2002) but the empirical data are very limited, and prospective studies with neuroimaging and a comprehensive battery of functional measures are needed. Matches.

§2.1, 2nd paragraph, proof lines 141-158, beginning on p. 2 and continuing on p. 3: distal axotomy as the predominant hypothesis; other interpretations including neuroadaptive change without terminal loss; the call for a clearer definition of neurotoxicity; and the cited authors' conclusion that MDMA can be considered neurotoxic in the sense of causing serotonergic dysfunction. Matches.

p. 1367, 9th (closing) paragraph: the modest deficits called entirely congruent with current understanding; the bio-energetic stress model with MDMA most damaging when taken intensively and cumulatively; and the conclusion that the study confirms MDMA's potential for causing neurobiological damage even when taken carefully. Matches, role supports.

Publisher HTML, 3rd and 4th paragraphs: evidence for functional signs remains mixed; transporter deficiencies appear to recover with abstinence while persisting years after fenfluramine; the two possibilities cannot be disentangled in retrospective studies; within-person comparison before and after controlled exposure is proposed, the limited examples to date showing no resulting deficits. The quotation is verbatim and 15 words. Role contradicts is right for this claim.

PMC HTML, 1st paragraph (considerable agreement on the need for well-controlled longitudinal studies) and 5th paragraph (large well-controlled prospective studies greatly needed to confirm or refute cross-sectional findings, while well-designed cross-sectional studies remain informative). Matches.

PMC HTML, 3rd paragraph: the critics combined the MDMA and control data in one correlation and found no association; the reply says low exposure falls somewhat below the control mean and high exposure above it, that the study enrolled people with 3 to 155 episodes, and that including controls obscures the dose-response relationship, which is evident with ranked data. No numbers are given for either analysis, as the anchor says.

corrected.extracted: The authors state that debate continues about the safety profile of MDMA, including whether possible serotonergic damage associated with recreational use is generalizable to pharmaceutical-grade MDMA (citing Doblin et al., 2014, and Parrott, 2013, 2014) and whether long-term neurocognitive deficits exist (citing Fisk et al., 2011; Halpern et al., 2004, 2011; Krebs et al., 2009; Lyvers, 2011; Lyvers and Hasking, 2004; Parrott, 2011). Of these, Halpern et al. (2011), Lyvers (2011) and Parrott (2011) are read in this batch; the Parrott (2013) cited here is a different paper (Human Psychopharmacology 28, 289-307), not the review carded as parrott_2013.

results.note: Place and role are right (p. 5, Discussion, 6th paragraph). The correction is to the extracted text: 'the reviews read in this batch' is wrong, because Barnett and Doblin's reference list gives Parrott (2013) as the Human Psychopharmacology overview, a different paper from the Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews review in this batch; the card already records this under its key finding 8.
